title: Plotting
text:
Two plots, answering different questions.
plot_motif_analysis shows the whole library: donor against recipient counts, one point per plasmid, with the carriers of each called motif highlighted, and beside it the log2FC distribution of each motif’s carriers against all plasmids. Plasmids absent from the recipient sit at y = 1, because a pseudocount is added before the log. It answers did this strain restrict anything, and does each call look like one shifted population rather than a handful of outliers.
plot_motif_depletion takes motifs you supply instead of the ones the pipeline found: a motif REBASE predicts for the strain, or one called in another strain. It tests a specific hypothesis, including when the answer is that the motif was not restricted.
Read either plot beside the result table, whose columns answer separate questions:

q_value: how sure we are that the carriers are depleted more than their background allows by chance — the depletion rate, in this sample, of plasmids with the same insert GC content. It grows with support, so a weak effect on many plasmids can be very significant.
fraction_depleted: how strong the effect is, the share of carriers depleted. For a weak motif, compare it with background (with all_motifs=True).
bimodality (with all_motifs=True): whether the carriers’ log2FC form one population or two. The row is flagged bimodal when they do (coefficient above 5/9) and one of the two groups is at background level: some carriers destroyed, others untouched, the signature of a motif that dilutes a different site.

The histogram shows log2FC as calculate_log2fc returns it, median-normalised: the median plasmid is at 0, and the pipeline’s default depletion threshold is at -0.5 on this axis.

title: randseq
text:
Usage
RandSeq conjugates a library of plasmids with random inserts from a donor into a recipient strain and counts each plasmid on both sides. A plasmid that carries a site the recipient’s defences recognise is lost. The example here, counts_panel.csv.gz, is a library of 150 nt random inserts counted in the donor (two replicates, Control_R1 and Control_R2) and in 8 recipient strains in two replicates each; counts_panel_key.csv says what each strain shows.

from randseq import calculate_log2fc, find_restricted_motifs, plot_motif_analysis, get_example_data_dir
import pandas as pd


# Read counts per plasmid: the donor library and 8 recipient strains, two replicates each
counts = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(get_example_data_dir(), "counts_panel.csv.gz"), index_col=0)
left, right = "GTCTAGGGCGGCGGTAAAAC", "ACTAGAGCACCAGAAGTCTA"   # vector sequence flanking the insert

# log2 fold change of each plasmid in each sample, against the first donor replicate
log2fc_df = calculate_log2fc(counts, reference_column="Control_R1")

find_restricted_motifs searches one sample’s log2 fold changes for the motifs whose carriers are depleted. It prints a log of its steps (not shown here) and returns the motifs it calls, in five columns. title: fast
text:
Without numba, one pattern is totalled by the numpy steps of 04_coding — window codes for every position of both strands, a sort per row to collapse repeats, and bincounts over what is left. Each step is a full pass over an intermediate array of n_sequences x 2 x insert length, and on a 30k-sequence library that is about 0.2 s per pattern. No single step dominates, so no numpy rewrite of one step buys much.
The kernel here fuses all of it into one compiled pass over the sequences. For each window it computes the code directly from the 2-bit bases, folds a self-reverse-complementary code onto min(code, rc) with the digit formula, and skips the window if this sequence has already counted that code — a stamp array recording the last sequence seen per code, which replaces the sort. What it accumulates is exactly what _motif_totals(*_motif_occurrences(...)) returns, so _scan_pattern can take either path and nothing downstream can tell which ran.
Measured on the 150 nt example library (counts_panel.csv.gz, 30,108 inserts after the count filter) over the 43 shipped patterns: numpy 8.7 s, this kernel 3.0 s on one core and 0.5 s on eight. The first call in a process also pays a one-off compile of about 4 s, cached on disk afterwards where the package directory is writable.


numba is not a hard dependency. Install it with the fast extra:
pip install "randseq[fast] @ git+https://github.com/dbikard/randseq.git"
Without it, HAVE_NUMBA is False and the scan runs the numpy path, which is the readable statement of the algorithm and the reference this kernel is tested against. Setting the environment variable RANDSEQ_NO_NUMBA=1 before importing randseq forces the numpy path even when numba is installed.

from randseq.coding import encode_library, _encode_motif


if HAVE_NUMBA:
    # the second sequence is the reverse complement of the first
    _enc = encode_library(["GAGACCTT", "AAGGTCTC", "TTTTTTTT"])
    n, n_dep, fc_sum, bg_sum, first = _pattern_totals(_enc, (6, 0, 0), [-3.0, -2.0, 0.5],
                                                     [0.25, 0.5, 0.125], log2FC_thr=-1)
    # (6, 0, 0) is self-rc, so GAGACC and GGTCTC fold onto the smaller code: both of the first two
    # sequences carry it, both are depleted, their backgrounds add, and the first carrier is 0
    _g = _encode_motif("GAGACC", (6, 0, 0))
    print("GAGACC: carriers", n[_g], " depleted", n_dep[_g], " log2FC sum", fc_sum[_g],
          " background sum", bg_sum[_g], " first carrier", first[_g])

GAGACC: carriers 2  depleted 2.0  log2FC sum -5.0  background sum 0.75  first carrier 0





The kernel re-implements every rule the numpy path applies — rejecting a window with a non-ACGT base or padding, folding the strands of a self-rc pattern, counting a motif once per sequence — so this notebook’s tests check each against _motif_occurrences + _motif_totals: on the example library for contiguous, balanced and asymmetric patterns, and on random ragged libraries containing N. tests/test_fast_scan.py repeats the comparison over all 43 shipped patterns, and runs the whole _get_pattern_scores both ways. Counts and background sums must agree exactly — plasmid_background returns multiples of 2⁻²⁰, which add exactly in any order — and the log2FC sums to 1e-9, since the threads add them in a different order.

title: core
text:
A library of plasmids carrying random inserts is conjugated into a recipient strain. A plasmid whose insert contains a site recognised by an active restriction system is destroyed on entry, so it is depleted relative to the input library. This module works back from each plasmid’s depletion to the motifs responsible.


Every plasmid gets a log2FC: how much rarer it became after delivery. Every motif gets the plasmids that contain it, and so a set of log2FC values. A motif’s score is the fraction of those values below a threshold — what fraction of the plasmids carrying this motif were destroyed. Everything after that is deciding which of the many motifs that score well is the actual site.
In steps:

counts → log2FC per plasmid
score every motif of every requested pattern — the scan
keep one description per site, discarding the same site written more or less specifically; set aside a candidate the vector flanks complete unless its sites inside the insert support it
drop a candidate whose score was borrowed from a stronger one
report each motif on its canonical strand, tested against the depletion of plasmids of the same GC content, with a degenerate site written as one IUPAC motif

Steps 3 and 4 are two halves of one problem: one real site makes many motifs score well. Step 3 compares motif strings; step 4 compares the plasmids motifs are found in, which relates descriptions too different for a string rule.




countsTable.csv.gz — 19 recipient strains, with the donor MFDpir as the input library; 11,629 inserts of 20 nt
counts_panel.csv.gz — 8 recipient strains and two donor replicates (Control_R1, Control_R2), each strain picked to exercise one behaviour of the pipeline (example_data/counts_panel_key.csv says which); 34,217 inserts, mostly 150 nt

E. coli JJ1886 is in both, so two measurements of one strain must agree on which motifs they call and on which strand they name them.

title: core
text:
Step 2: score every motif
Every motif of every pattern is scored over left_flank + insert + right_flank, on both strands. A pattern is the shape of a site, (d1, spacer, d2): defined bases, undefined gap, defined bases. (6, 0, 0) is a contiguous site like GGTCTC; (3, 4, 4) a bipartite site like CACNNNNGTAT. get_patterns() returns the shapes REBASE records for Type I, II and III systems; a site whose shape is not searched cannot be found.
The flanks are scanned because a site can straddle the junction between insert and vector. In the 150 nt panel library the left flank ends in AAAC, so every insert that starts NNNNGTC completes B156’s site AAACNNNNGTC: 382 of the 894 plasmids that carry the site in B156 carry it across the junction.
A motif is counted once per plasmid, however often it occurs there, and a motif and its reverse complement are one motif. Thresholds keep one convention throughout the package: a log2FC threshold is strict (log2FC < thr), a score or support threshold inclusive (>= thr, so min_support=3 means three supporting plasmids, not four).
Step 2 for one motif, by hand: GAGACC is in the first two sequences, in the second read on the other strand as GGTCTC.

_seqs = ["GAGACCTT", "AAGAGACC", "TTTTTTTT"]
_fc = [-2.0, 0.5, -3.0]

carries = [("GAGACC" in s) or ("GGTCTC" in s) for s in _seqs]   # either strand, one motif
vals = [f for f, c in zip(_fc, carries) if c]
print(f"plasmids carrying GAGACC : {[s for s, c in zip(_seqs, carries) if c]}")
print(f"their log2FC             : {vals}")
print(f"score, fraction below -1 : {np.mean(np.array(vals) < -1)}")

The scan does this for every motif of every pattern at once, on integer codes rather than strings: 04_coding shows how, and 05_fast adds an optional compiled kernel. Both are tested to give exactly the table of a readable string-based scan (tests/reference_scan.py).

On the example library
From here on the examples use JJ1886 in the 20 nt library: the inserts with their flanks (get_lib_seq_context), their log2FC, and each plasmid’s background — the depletion rate of plasmids of similar insert GC content, which every test is taken against (plasmid_background in 01_utils explains why). _scan_candidates scans one pattern and keeps the motifs that pass the support and score thresholds. It returns three things: the candidates, with motif, fraction_depleted, num_sequences, avg_log2fc, p_value and pattern (as a string); the p-value of every motif with enough support to be a test, survivor or not; and the pattern’s totals from _scan_pattern, so that later steps look motifs of this pattern up rather than scan it again. The p-values are returned because the Benjamini-Hochberg correction needs the full set of tests, and only this step sees it: a motif that fails the score threshold was still tested.

Step 3: one description per site
The scan returns one site described several ways. In this library the Type I site CACNNNNGTAT also comes back as CACNNNNGTA, one base shorter, and CACNNNNGTAC comes back once for each base pinned at the first position of its spacer (CACANNNGTAC, CACCNNNGTAC, …). Step 3 keeps one description per site, with one tool and three rules applied in this order:

the variant profile: pin one position next to a motif to each of A, C, G and T, and score the four motifs
rule 1, a mixture is not a site: drop a motif when some position next to it splits its four variants into depleting and not
rule 2, a one-base extension of a site is redundant: drop a motif that is a rule-1 survivor plus one defined base
rule 3, a motif with an uninformative base is not the site: drop a motif when putting N back at one of its defined bases gives four bases that all behave like the site


The variant profile
_variant_profile scores a set of related motifs — typically the four bases at one position — from the counts step 2 made (_scan_pattern), so a variant is scored exactly as the scan scored it, and a pattern is scanned at most once however many motifs need it. The counts are kept in totals, a dict by canonical pattern that holds for one library, log2FC, background and threshold; the pipeline shares it across calls, so a pattern step 2 scanned is never scanned again. A motif that has no code — an IUPAC letter, or a defined base in the spacer — gets n = 0 and nan for its score and background.

def _is_extension(specific, general):
    """Is `specific` the motif `general` with one more defined base, on either strand?

    The extra base sits one past an end of `general` or at an edge of its spacer -- the
    positions `_undefined_positions` tests. Both strands are checked because every pattern is
    searched in one canonical form, so adding a base to a motif's longer side can turn its shape
    into the mirror form, which the scan writes on the other strand: `TACNNNNGTGA` is
    `CACNNNNGTA` with a base added on the left.
    """
    defined = lambda m: len(m) - m.count("N")
    return defined(specific) == defined(general) + 1 and _find_broad_in_specific(specific, general)

Rule 3: a motif with an uninformative base is not the site
Rule 2 needs the shorter motif to be a candidate. When it fell short of the thresholds, a longer motif can still clear them because its extra base happens to pick out the most depleted of the shorter one’s carriers. Rule 3 asks from the other side: put N back at one of a candidate’s defined bases and classify the other three bases there. If every one behaves like the site, the candidate’s base carries no information.
A base is classified by comparing two models of its carriers — depleted at the site’s rate, or at their own background — by their log-likelihood ratio, which grows with the number of plasmids and so is also the confidence: a base is classified when one model fits ten times better. Simpler criteria fail: a fixed cut-off between the two rates misplaces the boundary, which depends on both, and a test against background calls site-like a base depleted at four times background but a quarter of the site’s rate. The site’s rate is the candidate’s own, re-estimated once from the candidate pooled with the bases first found site-like, because a candidate selected for scoring high overstates it.
Rule 3 drops a motif when, at one position, every other base is site-like. When only some are, the position is degenerate, and reporting writes it as an IUPAC letter (below).
The positions tested (_relax_positions) are those rule 1 tests from the other side: every base of a contiguous motif, an interior one becoming a one-base spacer, and for a gapped motif the outer and the spacer-side base of each half, as long as the half keeps a defined base. _classify_bases classifies the bases at one position; _classify_positions does it at each position asked, profiling a motif of A, C, G and T from the scan’s counts (_variant_profile) and one with an IUPAC letter on the carriers of its instances (_union_profile).

Beside them sits AATANNNNTGTG, 0.99 depleted on 190 plasmids, because nearly every plasmid that carries it also carries ATACNNNNGTG; the other 28 survivors are on seven plasmids or fewer. None of them is a site plus one base, so no string rule relates them to a site: that is step 4’s question.


Sites completed by the flank
Reading the flanks with each insert has a cost. The flank is the same in every plasmid, so where a motif uses flank bases it is a shorter motif of the insert at one fixed position, and whatever depletes those inserts scores for the motif too. Without this check, TA249 and ROAR8 in the 20 nt library are called for DCAANNNNNNTAGA, on 159 carriers; 157 of them read its TAGA in the right flank (GTTTTAGAGC…), so on them the motif is DCAA at insert positions 15–18. A real site completed by the flank also restricts where it lies wholly inside the insert: JJ1886’s RTACNNNNGTG needs the flank on 199 of its 212 carriers, and its 13 internal carriers are all depleted.
So a candidate that needs the flank on more than half its carriers (junction_share > 0.5) must stand on its internal carriers, those with a site wholly inside the insert, by the tests a call passes: at least min_support of them, the lower bound on their depleted fraction at score_thr, and their depleted count significant against their background (p < q_threshold). At 0.5 or below the internal carriers are at least half the support and the call already rests on them, so the trigger is fixed. The check runs between steps 3 and 4: step 4 lets a stronger candidate claim a weaker one’s plasmids, and a candidate the flank completes would claim them as readily as a site. _carriers(..., inside=True) reads the internal carriers off the windows that find the carriers: a window is inside the insert when it starts after one flank and ends before the other.

Step 4: drop candidates whose score was borrowed
Two descriptions of one site in different shapes — ATACNNNNGTG of pattern (4, 4, 3) and CACANNAGTA of (4, 2, 4) — sit on mostly the same plasmids, but neither is the other with a position left undefined. What separates them is what each has that the other does not:

    alone = _has[:, j] & ~_has[:, other]
    print(f"{_pair[j]:<12} n={_has[:, j].sum()}  score {_dep[_has[:, j]].mean():.3f}   "

Without the plasmids carrying ATACNNNNGTG, CACANNAGTA falls from 0.99 to 0.50: its score was borrowed. Without those carrying CACANNAGTA, ATACNNNNGTG holds at 1.00. A candidate is dropped when, restricted to the plasmids that carry it but no stronger candidate, it no longer reaches score_thr. The test is on the collapse, not on what is left: both leftovers here are four plasmids.
Candidates are tested strongest first — highest fraction depleted, then most plasmids — each against the union of the survivors ranked above it. Every survivor is then tested again against all the others, weakest first, because a shadow can rank above the site it shadows. A leftover must also be depleted beyond its own background at the scan’s cutoff: the largest p-value that clears q_threshold after Benjamini-Hochberg over every motif the scan tested, the pool every candidate was selected from. title: core
text:
Reporting
A motif and its reverse complement carry identical statistics, so each reported motif is put on its canonical strand (canonical_motif, 01_utils), its pattern mirrored to follow it: a site comes back as GGTCTC, never GAGACC, in every run and every dataset of the same strain.

Is the depletion one population or two?
A real site shifts its carriers as one population. A shadow of another site is a mixture: the carriers that also carry the real site are destroyed, the rest untouched. Sarle’s bimodality coefficient exceeds 5/9, its value for a uniform distribution, when a distribution has two modes — but also when the carriers fall into two depleted groups: CACNNNNGTAC on the 20 nt JJ1886 library has 19 carriers between −6.6 and −4.4 and one at −8.6, a coefficient of 0.654. So bimodal also requires that, split in two where they separate best, the upper group is not depleted (its median at or above log2fc_thr); bimodality keeps the raw coefficient. A shadow is significant and bimodal, a weak real site significant and unimodal, so both are reported; bimodality does not block a call.
_annotate_significance adds these two columns to the result table, with the p- and q-values and the bound on the depleted fraction (Reading the result table, below).


A degenerate site is one motif
The scan reports motifs of A, C, G and T, so a site that accepts two bases at a position comes back as two motifs. B156 in the example panel recognises GACNNNNGTTY; steps 2–4 call GAACNNNNGTC and AAACNNNNGTC — the site read on the other strand, split at its first base — and keep both, because each depletes plasmids the other does not carry. Rule 3’s classification reads the position:

counts_panel = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(data_path, "counts_panel.csv.gz"), index_col=0)
left_panel, right_panel = "GTCTAGGGCGGCGGTAAAAC", "ACTAGAGCACCAGAAGTCTA"
log2fc_panel = calculate_log2fc(counts_panel, reference_column="Control_R1", count_threshold=20)
b156 = log2fc_panel["B156_R1"]
enc_panel = encode_library(get_lib_seq_context(b156.index.tolist(), left_panel, right_panel))
fc_b156 = b156.to_numpy()
bg_b156 = plasmid_background(b156.index, fc_b156, -0.5)

_cls = _classify_positions("GAACNNNNGTC", [0], (4, 4, 3), enc_panel, fc_b156, bg_b156, -0.5)[0]
for m, n, s, b in _variant_profile([x + "AACNNNNGTC" for x in "ACGT"], (4, 4, 3), enc_panel,
                                  fc_b156, bg_b156, -0.5):
    print(f"  {m}  n={n:>4}  score={s:.3f}  background={b:.3f}  {_cls.get(m[0], ('(the call)',))[0]}")

One other base is site-like and two are not, so the position is degenerate and becomes R. _generalise_motif applies this to every defined position of a call, one position at a time — the one whose site-like bases have the most carriers, the first on a tie — and classifies the merged motif again on its own carriers until nothing changes. A merged motif’s carriers are the plasmids carrying any of its instances, counted from the presence matrix, since one plasmid can carry two.

A palindromic site has a limit of its own. In CCTNAGG (381A) the central N pairs C with G and A with T, so CCTHAGG (not G, hence not C on the other strand) is carried by exactly the plasmids carrying CCTNAGG: the data can only set C/G against A/T. In both 381A replicates A/T is site-like beside C/G, so CCTNAGG is what the data support.

Reading the result table
find_restricted_motifs returns the called motifs in five columns: motif, num_sequences, fraction_depleted, avg_log2fc and q_value. With all_motifs=True it returns every motif that reached scoring, called or not, with all the columns below.

How strong is the effect? fraction_depleted is the share of carriers depleted, and avg_log2fc says how far they fall. Compare fraction_depleted with background, the rate at which plasmids like the carriers deplete anyway (plasmid_background): 381A’s CCTNAGG depletes 0.74 of its carriers against a background of 0.30 (The example panel at a glance, below), EDL933’s CACNNNNNNNCTGG 0.91 against 0.09.
How sure are we? p_value is the binomial probability of at least this many depleted carriers at their background rate, and q_value adjusts it over every motif the scan tested in the sample (01_utils, Is a motif’s depletion more than the sample’s own noise?). A call needs q < q_threshold.
Are most carriers depleted? fraction_depleted_lower is a 95% lower bound on the depleted fraction, and a call needs it at score_thr too. On the 20 nt JJ1886 library CTTNCACA has 10 of 20 carriers depleted (q = 7·10⁻⁵) but bounds the fraction only at 0.30; GGTCTC, 9 of 9, bounds it at 0.72.
Does it need the flank? junction_share is the share of carriers with no site wholly inside the insert. Above 0.5 a call also needs its internal_n internal carriers to pass on their own: internal_fraction_lower at score_thr, internal_p_value below q_threshold (Sites completed by the flank). A candidate that fails this is listed only when it would otherwise be called.
Is it one population? bimodal marks carriers that mix destroyed and untouched plasmids; bimodality is the raw coefficient.
Is it a degenerate site? merged_from lists the variants an IUPAC motif replaced, and is empty for every other row.
Why called or not? called is the verdict, and reason (call_reason) says it in words: called, or each test that failed with its numbers. A called row whose carriers are bimodal says so, since that is worth a look before trusting the call.

find_restricted_motifs expects log2FC as calculate_log2fc returns them, median-normalised, and uses them as given: normalise values computed elsewhere the same way. Every test is against the GC-matched background of plasmid_background. On the arguments:

log2fc_thr, −0.5 by default, is relative to the sample’s median plasmid: low enough to see weakly restricting systems such as BREX, which −1 misses.
min_support: with every carrier depleted, the lower bound on the depleted fraction is 0.22, 0.37, 0.47 and 0.55 for 2 to 5 carriers, so 5 is the smallest support that can be called at score_thr=0.5 (4 at 0.45, 7 at 0.65). Lower only adds candidates and runtime: E1114 on the 20 nt library exceeds max_candidates at 2 to 4.
score_thr: a candidate needs this share of its carriers depleted, and a call needs the lower bound fraction_depleted_lower to reach it.
q_threshold: the q-value is Benjamini-Hochberg over every motif the scan tested, each against its carriers’ background.
max_candidates: step 4’s cost grows faster than the number of candidates. The default, 5000, is above the 3,258 that the busiest strain of the example data (E1114, 20 nt library) brings at the defaults. A caller screening many strains should catch TooManyCandidatesError and record that strain as “no confident call”.
patterns: a pattern and its mirror find the same sites, so each is searched once, in one form: (4, 4, 3) is searched as (3, 4, 4).
n_jobs: a pattern takes about a second on a 30k-sequence library, so more processes are rarely worth their startup cost.

encoded_library: encode_library(get_lib_seq_context(log2fc_series.index, left, right)). Strains screened with the same library and flanks share it, so a panel encodes it once; it must describe exactly log2fc_series.index, in order.

title: Utils
text:
Each plasmid’s depletion is the log2 ratio of its share of the recipient sample to its share of the donor library, normalised so that the sample’s median plasmid sits at 0. Four details matter:

The pseudocount is added to raw counts, before normalisation: (n+1)/Σ(n+1) per sample, then the ratio. Normalised counts are far below 1, so adding 1 after normalising would flatten every ratio towards 1.
Shares are over the plasmids that pass the count filter, not over every molecule sequenced. That is a per-sample constant: it shifts all log2FC of a sample by the same amount, and the median normalisation below removes it.
Each sample is normalised to its median plasmid (normalize="median", the default): each column’s median log2FC is subtracted, so the median plasmid has log2FC 0, a fold change of 1. This is median-ratio normalisation, as in DESeq2; on the log2 scale, subtracting the median is the same as rescaling the counts by the median ratio. Shares alone are not enough: when a few plasmids take a large share of a sample’s reads, every other plasmid’s share shrinks and its log2FC falls below 0, by an amount that differs from strain to strain. Against the median plasmid, a depletion threshold of −0.5 means the same in every strain. normalize="total" stops at the shares.
The filter is reference count > count_threshold (default 20), in the one reference column.

count_threshold filters on donor abundance, not on depletion, so raising it costs power but does not choose which motifs are called. It does set how many plasmids carry each motif, so num_sequences is comparable between experiments only at the same threshold.

section: Choosing which strand to report a motif on
text:
Choosing which strand to report a motif on
A recognition site and its reverse complement are the same site. The library is scanned on both strands, so a motif and its reverse complement always get identical statistics — same number of supporting sequences, same depletion score, same average log2FC. They are one answer, and which spelling to report is a tie that has to be broken the same way every time, or two result tables cannot be compared (GAGACC in one, GGTCTC in the other).
canonical_motif reports the strand REBASE uses, so results line up with the literature and with enzyme names (GGTCTC is BsaI/Eco31I). For motifs REBASE does not know, which includes most of what a discovery screen finds, it falls back to the alphabetically first strand: arbitrary, but the same on every run and machine. A motif REBASE lists on both strands takes the alphabetically first too.

title: Utils
text:
The search space
A pattern (d1, spacer, d2) is the shape of a site: defined bases, undefined gap, defined bases. get_patterns returns the shapes the scan searches by default, each in the one form the scan uses.
The default is 43 patterns: contiguous sites of 5–7 bases, and gapped sites whose halves are 2–4 bases, with 5–8 defined bases in all and a gap of 1–8. It fits 837 of the 983 distinct motifs in the REBASE Gold Standard set shipped with the package. The arguments widen it: get_patterns(contiguous=(4, 8), halves=(2, 5), max_spacer=9) (68 patterns) fits 902, and adding max_defined=9 (77) fits 911, at about 8 times the motifs tested (3.6 million against 460,000 on the larger example library). That is not the default because, at the default thresholds, a wider search adds one-base-longer descriptions of weak or degenerate sites that steps 3 and 4 do not yet catch.
A site whose half has an undefined base inside it, such as CNGTANNNNNNTTC, has two gaps, and no pattern describes it: 47 of the 983 Gold Standard motifs are of this kind, almost all Type I. Each concrete variant of such a site has a one-gap shape, here (5, 6, 3), which can be passed in patterns to find the site. The variants are then reported as separate rows (CAGTANNNNNNTTC, CCGTANNNNNNTTC, …), because writing N inside a half would give a shape the scan does not search.

section: Is a motif’s depletion more than the sample’s own noise?
text:
Is a motif’s depletion more than the sample’s own noise?
The scan in 00_core tests a great many motifs (about 330,000 with the default 5 or more supporting plasmids on the smaller example library, 460,000 on the larger), so some will look perfect by luck alone. How many supporting plasmids a call needs before that stops being a plausible explanation depends on the sample, not on a constant.
Under the null, a motif’s depleted count is Binomial(n, p) where p is the rate at which its carriers would deplete in this sample if no site were involved: their background. A noisy sample has a higher p and therefore needs more evidence for the same claim, automatically. How p is estimated for each motif is the next section; first, the binomial form itself.
Shuffled data bear this out. With each sample’s log2FC shuffled across its plasmids, 20 times for each of six strains of the two example libraries, find_restricted_motifs at the defaults calls nothing, at any min_support from 2 to 6; the smallest q in any shuffle is 0.005, on a row the confidence bound rejects.
What this does not model. The binomial treats the plasmids carrying a motif as independent draws. They are not: motifs co-occur, which is the whole subject of step 4 of the core pipeline. So the p-value is a screen against chance, not a complete model of how a spurious call arises: a shadow of a real site is highly significant by this test and still needs explaining away.

title: coding
text:
The scan in 00_core scores every motif of every pattern against every sequence, which is where its runtime goes. On strings — a Python set of motif strings per sequence — that costs roughly 10 s and 2 GB of RAM per pattern on a 30k-sequence library; on integers it is well under a second.
A motif of pattern (d1, spacer, d2) is pinned down entirely by its d1 + d2 defined bases — the spacer is N by construction — so it can be held as an integer in [0, 4**(d1+d2)). Every per-motif statistic then becomes an np.bincount over those integers, and the library is encoded once and reused for every pattern.
Nothing here decides anything biological: its only job is to give exactly the answer a readable string-based scan would, faster. The checks in this notebook hold the encoding to that, and tests/test_reference_scan.py holds the whole scan to it.


A=0, C=1, G=2, T=3, and anything else — N, lowercase junk, the padding of a short sequence — is 4.
The order is not arbitrary. Complementary bases sit at opposite ends of it, so complementing a base is 3 - code: A↔︎T is 0↔︎3, C↔︎G is 1↔︎2. That is the whole reverse-complement implementation, and it is why encode_library can return the reverse strand for the price of one subtraction and one reversal.
Code 4 does double duty: it marks a base that is not ACGT and the padding that squares off a ragged library into a rectangular array. Both must be excluded from the scan, and because they share a marker, one test excludes both — there is no separate length bookkeeping to get wrong.

Both strands are left-aligned and padded on the right, so row i of rc is the reverse complement of sequence i occupying its first len(s) columns — not a reversal of the padded row, which would put the padding at the front.



Write the d1 + d2 defined bases of a motif as the digits of a base-4 numeral:
CAC NNNN GTAT   ->  digits C,A,C,G,T,A,T  ->  1·4⁶ + 0·4⁵ + 1·4⁴ + 2·4³ + 3·4² + 0·4 + 3
_pattern_window_codes builds that numeral by Horner’s method — code = code*4 + next_digit, one pass over the defined positions in increasing order. The trick that makes it fast is that each step operates on a sliding view, encoded_seqs[:, j:j+n_windows]: position j of the window starting at w is absolute index w+j, so as w runs over all windows that column is exactly the slice above. Every window of every sequence is therefore built in parallel, with one vector operation per defined base rather than one per window.
Rejecting windows. A window containing a non-ACGT base anywhere — spacer included, to match the [ATGC] regex the reference implementation uses — is set to 4**(d1+d2), one past the largest real code. Which windows those are comes from a prefix sum over the == 4 mask: the number of bad bases in [w, w+width) is n_bad[w+width] - n_bad[w], so all windows are tested at once. Padding is code 4, so a window running off the end of a short sequence is rejected by the same test, with nothing extra written for it.
Decoding reverses the numeral. Base 4 is two bits, so digit i counted from the most significant is (code >> 2*(n-1-i)) & 3 — the same digits in the same order the encoder wrote them. _decode_motif_codes then drops N into the spacer positions.
With pattern (1, 2, 2), CAAGT has a single window whose defined bases are C, G, T, i.e. code 1*16 + 2*4 + 3 = 27. A window touching the N is rejected (code 4**3 = 64):

fwd, rc = encode_library(["CAAGT", "CAAGTN"])

# A=0 C=1 G=2 T=3, so a motif's code is literally its defined bases as a base-4 numeral:
# CNNGT of pattern (1,2,2) has defined bases C,G,T -> digits 1,2,3 -> int("123", 4).
CNNGT = int("123", 4)
REJECTED = 4 ** 3            # the sentinel: one past the largest 3-digit base-4 numeral
print(f"CNNGT = {CNNGT}, REJECTED = {REJECTED}")
print(_pattern_window_codes(fwd, (1, 2, 2)))
_decode_motif_codes([CNNGT, int("000", 4)], (1, 2, 2))

CNNGT = 27, REJECTED = 64
[[27 64]
 [27 64]]


['CNNGT', 'ANNAA']





The scan reports a motif string, but everything between the library and that string is integer arithmetic. Four properties have to hold, or the output is confidently wrong rather than obviously broken.
1. Distinct motifs get distinct codes. A base-4 numeral with a fixed number of digits is unique to its digit string — that is just positional notation — and the digit count is fixed at d1+d2 for a given pattern. Two different motifs of the same pattern therefore cannot collide.
2. Decoding is exactly the inverse of encoding. Both walk the same d1+d2 positions in the same order; the encoder multiplies up, the decoder shifts down. Cheap enough to check exhaustively rather than argue about, which this notebook’s tests do.
3. A rejected window can never be read as a motif. Real codes fill [0, 4**(d1+d2)) and the sentinel is 4**(d1+d2) exactly, so the single test code < 4**(d1+d2) separates them with no gap and no overlap. This is why the sentinel is that value and not, say, -1.
4. The arithmetic stays in range. Codes are int32, which holds 15 defined bases; the shipped patterns use at most 8. Beyond 15 the numeral would wrap and every count for that pattern would be quietly wrong, so _pattern_window_codes raises instead.
Properties 1–3 hold by construction and are verified exhaustively by this notebook’s tests. Whether the whole scan means the same thing as a readable implementation is a separate question: tests/test_reference_scan.py runs _get_pattern_scores against the string-based scan in tests/reference_scan.py and requires identical tables.



_encode_motif is the inverse of _decode_motif_codes: it turns a motif string back into the integer the scan counts under. It returns None for anything it cannot represent — an IUPAC-degenerate motif has no single code, and nor has a motif that does not fit the pattern — so a caller can expand a degenerate motif into its instances (_motif_instances in core) or fall back to a regex, rather than silently mis-assign sequences. tests/test_vectorized_presence.py checks the two paths agree element for element.

# the decode example above, inverted: CNNGT is digits 1,2,3; an IUPAC base has no single code
_encode_motif("CNNGT", (1, 2, 2)), _encode_motif("YNNGT", (1, 2, 2))

(27, None)





An enzyme cuts a double-stranded site, so GAGACC and GGTCTC are one motif seen from two sides, and the scan must not count them as two. Where they can be folded together is decided by the pattern, because a motif of (d1, spacer, d2) reverse-complements into one of (d2, spacer, d1):

when that is the same shape — a contiguous motif (spacer == 0), or a balanced one (d1 == d2) — both spellings are codes in the same space, and one physical site is found twice, once per strand. These fold.
otherwise the rc spelling lives in another pattern’s space. Nothing to fold: scanning (3, 4, 4) on both strands already finds each site exactly once, because a (4, 4, 3) site is read on the reverse strand and spelled as (3, 4, 4). This is why find_restricted_motifs rewrites every pattern to its _canonical_pattern and drops duplicates — searching both shapes would re-find the same sites in mirror spelling, at twice the cost.

Folding an asymmetric pattern would merge two unrelated motifs, since reversing the digits of a (4, 4, 3) code reads the d2 bases where the d1 bases belong. _rc_code_table therefore refuses any pattern that is not self-rc.
The table itself is one observation: a code is the defined bases as a base-4 numeral, and the defined bases of the reverse complement are those digits reversed and complemented (A<->T, C<->G is 3 - digit). The spacer is undefined on both strands, so it plays no part. Because each base is two bits, both operations are bit arithmetic on the code: complementing every digit is a single XOR with 11 repeated k times, and reversing the digits is reversing the order of the 2-bit groups. _rc_code_table builds the table that way, and this notebook’s tests check it against revcomp on the motif strings over entire code spaces.

# GAGACC and GGTCTC are one site: the table maps each spelling's code to the other's
_t = _rc_code_table((6, 0, 0))
print(_decode_motif_codes([_t[_encode_motif("GAGACC", (6, 0, 0))]], (6, 0, 0)))
# contiguous and balanced patterns fold; (3, 4, 4) does not, its rc motifs are (4, 4, 3)
[_pattern_is_self_rc(p) for p in [(6, 0, 0), (4, 4, 4), (3, 4, 4)]]

Which windows those are comes from a prefix sum over the == 4 mask: the number of bad bases in [w, w+width) is n_bad[w+width] - n_bad[w], so all windows are tested at once. Padding is code 4, so a window running off the end of a short sequence is rejected by the same test, with nothing extra written for it.
Decoding reverses the numeral. Base 4 is two bits, so digit i counted from the most significant is (code >> 2*(n-1-i)) & 3 — the same digits in the same order the encoder wrote them. _decode_motif_codes then drops N into the spacer positions.
With pattern (1, 2, 2), CAAGT has a single window whose defined bases are C, G, T, i.e. code 1*16 + 2*4 + 3 = 27. A window touching the N is rejected (code 4**3 = 64):

fwd, rc = encode_library(["CAAGT", "CAAGTN"])

# A=0 C=1 G=2 T=3, so a motif's code is literally its defined bases as a base-4 numeral:
# CNNGT of pattern (1,2,2) has defined bases C,G,T -> digits 1,2,3 -> int("123", 4).
CNNGT = int("123", 4)
REJECTED = 4 ** 3            # the sentinel: one past the largest 3-digit base-4 numeral
print(f"CNNGT = {CNNGT}, REJECTED = {REJECTED}")
print(_pattern_window_codes(fwd, (1, 2, 2)))
_decode_motif_codes([CNNGT, int("000", 4)], (1, 2, 2))

CNNGT = 27, REJECTED = 64
[[27 64]
 [27 64]]


['CNNGT', 'ANNAA']





The scan reports a motif string, but everything between the library and that string is integer arithmetic. Four properties have to hold, or the output is confidently wrong rather than obviously broken.
1. Distinct motifs get distinct codes. A base-4 numeral with a fixed number of digits is unique to its digit string — that is just positional notation — and the digit count is fixed at d1+d2 for a given pattern. Two different motifs of the same pattern therefore cannot collide.
2. Decoding is exactly the inverse of encoding. Both walk the same d1+d2 positions in the same order; the encoder multiplies up, the decoder shifts down. Cheap enough to check exhaustively rather than argue about, which this notebook’s tests do.
3. A rejected window can never be read as a motif. Real codes fill [0, 4**(d1+d2)) and the sentinel is 4**(d1+d2) exactly, so the single test code < 4**(d1+d2) separates them with no gap and no overlap. This is why the sentinel is that value and not, say, -1.
4. The arithmetic stays in range. Codes are int32, which holds 15 defined bases; the shipped patterns use at most 8. Beyond 15 the numeral would wrap and every count for that pattern would be quietly wrong, so _pattern_window_codes raises instead.
Properties 1–3 hold by construction and are verified exhaustively by this notebook’s tests. Whether the whole scan means the same thing as a readable implementation is a separate question: tests/test_reference_scan.py runs _get_pattern_scores against the string-based scan in tests/reference_scan.py and requires identical tables.



_encode_motif is the inverse of _decode_motif_codes: it turns a motif string back into the integer the scan counts under. It returns None for anything it cannot represent — an IUPAC-degenerate motif has no single code, and nor has a motif that does not fit the pattern — so a caller can expand a degenerate motif into its instances (_motif_instances in core) or fall back to a regex, rather than silently mis-assign sequences. tests/test_vectorized_presence.py checks the two paths agree element for element.

# the decode example above, inverted: CNNGT is digits 1,2,3; an IUPAC base has no single code
_encode_motif("CNNGT", (1, 2, 2)), _encode_motif("YNNGT", (1, 2, 2))

(27, None)





An enzyme cuts a double-stranded site, so GAGACC and GGTCTC are one motif seen from two sides, and the scan must not count them as two. Where they can be folded together is decided by the pattern, because a motif of (d1, spacer, d2) reverse-complements into one of (d2, spacer, d1):

when that is the same shape — a contiguous motif (spacer == 0), or a balanced one (d1 == d2) — both spellings are codes in the same space, and one physical site is found twice, once per strand. These fold.
otherwise the rc spelling lives in another pattern’s space. Nothing to fold: scanning (3, 4, 4) on both strands already finds each site exactly once, because a (4, 4, 3) site is read on the reverse strand and spelled as (3, 4, 4). This is why find_restricted_motifs rewrites every pattern to its _canonical_pattern and drops duplicates — searching both shapes would re-find the same sites in mirror spelling, at twice the cost.

Folding an asymmetric pattern would merge two unrelated motifs, since reversing the digits of a (4, 4, 3) code reads the d2 bases where the d1 bases belong. _rc_code_table therefore refuses any pattern that is not self-rc.
The table itself is one observation: a code is the defined bases as a base-4 numeral, and the defined bases of the reverse complement are those digits reversed and complemented (A<->T, C<->G is 3 - digit). The spacer is undefined on both strands, so it plays no part. Because each base is two bits, both operations are bit arithmetic on the code: complementing every digit is a single XOR with 11 repeated k times, and reversing the digits is reversing the order of the 2-bit groups. _rc_code_table builds the table that way, and this notebook’s tests check it against revcomp on the motif strings over entire code spaces.

# GAGACC and GGTCTC are one site: the table maps each spelling's code to the other's
_t = _rc_code_table((6, 0, 0))
print(_decode_motif_codes([_t[_encode_motif("GAGACC", (6, 0, 0))]], (6, 0, 0)))
# contiguous and balanced patterns fold; (3, 4, 4) does not, its rc motifs are (4, 4, 3)
[_pattern_is_self_rc(p) for p in [(6, 0, 0), (4, 4, 4), (3, 4, 4)]]

['GGTCTC']

title: coding
section: Reading motif presence off the window codes
text:
Reading motif presence off the window codes
Scoring a pattern asks what motifs a sequence contains. The rest of the pipeline asks the reverse, of a handful of specific candidates: which sequences contain this motif, on either strand?
Done directly that is a regex per sequence per motif, and a noisy strain, which carries the most candidates, pays for it most. Instead presence is a lookup in the window codes, done once per pattern rather than once per motif: for 200 motifs of 4 patterns on the 150 nt example library (counts_panel.csv.gz, 30,108 inserts after the count filter), 0.3 s against 6 s for the regex, with identical answers.
_motif_presence_matrix returns (matrix, handled). A motif the fast path cannot encode — IUPAC-degenerate, or of an unknown pattern — is left as an all-False column and flagged in handled, so the caller does not read a blank column as “absent”: core reads a degenerate motif through its instances, each of which has a code, and a motif of unknown pattern by regex.
With insert (the lengths of the two flanks and of each insert) it also says which sequences carry the motif wholly inside the insert, from the same windows: this is how core tells a site from one the vector flank completes (Sites completed by the flank).

_seqs = ["GAGACCTT", "AAGGTCTC", "TTTTTTTT", "GGGGGGGG"]
_m, _handled = _motif_presence_matrix(encode_library(_seqs), ["GAGACC", "TTTTTT"],
                                     [(6, 0, 0), (6, 0, 0)])
